title: Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests
subtitle: From a sample to a statement about the population — with an honest measure of how wrong we might be.

sections.title: Estimation
sections.body: A statistic computed from a sample estimates a population parameter: x̄ for μ, s² for σ² (÷(n − 1) makes it unbiased), p̂ for p. A good estimator is unbiased (right on average) and has small standard error σ/√n — more data tightens it.

questions.prompt: Why divide by n − 1 in the sample variance?

choices.text: It makes the answer bigger for fun.
It makes s² unbiased for σ².

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: x̄ is fitted from the same data, using up one degree of freedom.

sections.title: Confidence interval for a mean
sections.body: With σ known (or n large): x̄ ± z·σ/√n, where z = 1.645, 1.96, 2.576 for 90 %, 95 %, 99 %. The 95 % means: if you repeated the whole sampling many times, about 95 % of the intervals built this way would contain μ. It is not a 95 % chance that μ lies in one given interval. Below, 100 simulated intervals at z = 1.96 caught the true mean 96% of the time; at z = 2.576 99% (wider, half-width 5.152 vs 3.92).

sections.title: Effect of n and confidence level
sections.body: Width = 2zσ/√n. Raising confidence raises z (wider). Raising n shrinks it: half-width is 3.92 at n = 25 but 1.96 at n = 100. Precision, confidence and cost pull against each other; you choose two.

sections.title: Hypothesis testing: the logic
sections.body: State a null hypothesis H₀ (“nothing special”, e.g. μ = μ₀) and an alternative H₁. Compute a test statistic, e.g. z = (x̄ − μ₀)/(σ/√n). If it falls in the rejection region (|z| > 1.96 at α = 0.05, two-sided) — equivalently if the p-value < α — reject H₀. Errors: Type I = rejecting a true H₀ (probability α); Type II = failing to reject a false H₀ (probability β; power = 1 − β).

choices.text: Keeping H₀ when it is false.
Rejecting H₀ when it is true.

sections.title: Worked test of a mean
sections.body: A maker claims a bulb lasts 1000 h (σ = 80). A sample of 64 averages 980 h. Is the claim still believable at α = 0.05?

questions.prompt: A p-value of 0.03 at α = 0.05 means…

choices.text: H₀ is 3 % likely to be true.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Data this extreme would occur only 3 % of the time if H₀ were true.

problems.prompt: H₀: μ = 50, σ = 6, n = 36, x̄ = 52. Two-sided test at 5 %.

sections.title: Unknown σ: the t-test
sections.body: When σ must be estimated by s, use t = (x̄ − μ₀)/(s/√n) with n − 1 degrees of freedom. The t distribution has heavier tails than the normal, so critical values are larger (2.262 at 9 d.f. vs 1.96) — the price of not knowing σ. As n grows, t → z. For two proportions or categorical counts the χ² test compares observed and expected counts: χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E.
